title: SQL Injection in product search endpoint
description: The /products/search endpoint builds an SQL query by concatenating the user-supplied q parameter directly into the SQL string using Python string formatting. This allows attackers to execute arbitrary SQL commands against the SQLite database.
evidence: GET /products/search?q='%20OR%201=1%20-- returned all 6 products instead of zero matching results, confirming SQL injection. Code: shopapi/products.py line 41: 'SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%" + q + "%' OR sku LIKE...

title: Stored SQL Injection in admin review report via display_name
description: The /admin/reports/reviews endpoint interpolates customer.display_name directly into SQL using f-string formatting (line 80), even though display_name comes from the database. An attacker can register with a crafted display_name containing SQL injection payloads, and when a staff member queries that customer's reviews, the payload executes. This is a stored SQL injection vector.
evidence: Code: shopapi/admin.py lines 77-80: f'SELECT r.id, p.name AS product, r.rating, r.body, r.created FROM reviews r JOIN products p ON p.id = r.product_id WHERE r.author_name = \'{customer[display_name]}\'. Stored injection via display_name set during registration at shopapi/auth.py line 71.

title: Token refresh endpoint skips signature verification allowing forgery
description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes JWT tokens with verify_signature=False, accepting any arbitrarily forged token. An attacker can supply a token with claims like sub=any_valid_user_id and get a fresh, legitimately signed token back, achieving full account takeover.
evidence: POST /auth/refresh with hand-crafted JWT containing sub=1 was accepted and returned a valid new token for user id=1. Code: shopapi/auth.py lines 98-107 where jwt.decode(token, options={verify_signature: False}) is called.

title: IDOR on order detail view allows viewing any user's orders
description: The GET /orders/<order_id> endpoint requires authentication but does not verify that the requesting user owns the order. Any authenticated user can view details of any other user's orders including items, prices, statuses and refund information.
evidence: GET /orders/3 as authenticated user with id=1 returned order belonging to user id=2, including item list, status and amounts. Code: shopapi/orders.py line 49 shows show_order() calls get_order() which only checks order existence, not ownership. own_order() function exists but is unused here.

title: CORS reflects untrusted Origin header with credentials enabled
description: The CORS after_request handler sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the exact value of the request Origin header without validation. Combined with CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS=True, this allows any origin to make credentialed cross-origin requests against the application.
evidence: GET request with Origin: https://evil.example.com received Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example.com and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Code: shopapi/__init__.py lines 44-51; config.py line 12.

title: Order auto-marked as paid on payment provider timeout
description: In confirm-payment(), when the payment provider times out, the code defaults status to paid and transitions the order to processing with paid_pence equal to total_pence. Orders can be fulfilled without actual payment confirmation simply by causing a network timeout to the provider.
evidence: Code: shopapi/payments.py lines 37-42. If client().payment_status() raises requests.Timeout, status is set to paid regardless of actual payment state, and order is updated to processing with paid_pence=total_pence.

title: Passwords stored with unsalted SHA-256 hash
description: hash_password uses plain SHA-256 without salt, making it vulnerable to rainbow table attacks and identical password detection across accounts. Modern applications should use bcrypt, argon2, or similar slow hashing functions.
evidence: Code: shopapi/auth.py line 16: hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(). No random salt applied. Used everywhere passwords are stored including registration (line 78) and password reset (line 159).

title: Password reset tokens have low entropy
description: Reset tokens are generated as %08d with int(random.random()*10**8), producing only 8 decimal digits with at most ~2^27 entropy using the predictable Mersenne Twister PRNG. Attackers can brute-force the space trivially.
evidence: Code: shopapi/auth.py line 135. Tokens are 8-digit numeric codes sent via email log mechanism. Brute-forcing 100 million possibilities is trivial.

title: Full request body logged for write operations exposing sensitive data
description: The log_request before_request handler logs the full request body up to 2000 chars for every POST, PUT and PATCH request. This includes login credentials, registration data, gift card codes and other sensitive input written to logs.
evidence: Code: shopapi/__init__.py lines 30-31: log.info(%s %s %s, request.method, request.path, request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000]). Sensitive endpoints include /auth/login, /auth/register, /giftcards/redeem.

title: Basket cookie uses pickle deserialization
description: The basket cookie is serialized/deserialized using Python pickle (line 20). While current exception handling returns empty dict on failure, pickle has known RCE gadget chains and is unsafe for untrusted data. Pickle usage also appears in cache.py for file-based caching.
evidence: Code: shopapi/basket.py line 20: pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)). Same pattern in cache.py lines 23 and 31 for on-disk cache files.
